utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. Mr. Tolimir, you may continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Of course, I have to remind the witness to tell the truth, and the affirmation still applies. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May Lord bless this house. I wish we all have a fruitful, successful work and that all days, including this one, during this trial be concluded according to God's wishes and not necessarily mine. A question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday, just before the end, we provided you with a list. I don't know whether you returned it to the Registrar.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You said that most of the people on the list were people from Zepa?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were those the people who refused to disarm, in keeping with the decision of the War Presidency of the 27th?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those were the people who were considered men of military age.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Save for the one for whom you said was killed, are the rest of them alive, have they survived the events in Srebrenica and Zepa?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they have. From what I know, from Serbia they were taken to third countries. Some returned to Bosnia eventually, whereas others stayed in their new countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know the percentage of those who left for third countries, as opposed to those who returned, be it immediately or after the war?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number. According to what I was able to hear, in late 1995 they were offered a number of countries, and the initial people left. I believe they went in several groups, not all at once. Of course, I must underline that this is what I heard only. Out of some 800 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were some 800 people in Serbia, but I don't know what percentage of them returned to Bosnia eventually. I don't want to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We saw the agreement, containing an item which states that freedom of movement will be guaranteed, and it was also stated that once the war was over, people would be allowed to go where they wished. We can see D51, if necessary. If you recall, General Mladic also addressed that issue at a meeting. You said that the Dayton Accords dealt with that issue and the people were free to return according to their wishes. Some people actually did return?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean people to Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Precisely. Then, during examination-in-chief, it was suggested that the Dayton Accords followed the events in Zepa quite late during the decade. What is your opinion on that?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was still in the prison, the Dayton Accords were already signed. I think they were verified and ratified, in terms of implementation, by way of, I think, the Paris Treaty. I think the whole thing was finished by December 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So it was in the same year when the agreement D51 was signed?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see D51 now, but we should be careful not to broadcast the page with the signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Therefore, that item concerning freedom of movement was reaffirmed through the Dayton Accords because it was a part of the overall peace process in Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was defined by the Dayton Accords. Perhaps we can say that these two things corresponded.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Who signed the Dayton Accords, the participants of the war in Bosnia or all three sides as well as international community representatives? What can you tell us? Apologies. Could we please remove the names from the screen. Perhaps scroll down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Registrar made sure this document would not be broadcast, because at the top and at the end, the name is to be seen. So that don't worry, it will not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I wasn't aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the Dayton Accords were signed by the participants, so to say, of the war. It was done under the auspices of the standing members of the Security Committee, I believe, although I'm not certain of that. And guarantees were also offered by Serbia and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know whether it also included an RS delegation?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know they participated in the work surrounding the accords, but I don't know whether they were the signatories as well. In any case, I know the delegation was in Dayton.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Not everyone signed, just those representing the actual countries. In any case, this is the umbrella agreement covering all of the other agreements that were eventually reached during the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the Dayton Accords have annexes regulating all matters at hand. In any case, all segments were covered, in terms of securing normal life and work, freedom of movement, a possibility of return, the organisation of state. All of those things were covered by the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In item 7, it says: "In accordance with the Geneva Conventions of 12 August 1949 and the Additional Protocols of 1977, the civilian population of Zepa shall be given the freedom to choose their place of residence while hostilities continue." Did the hostilities cease immediately afterwards, in September, when the Dayton talks began?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was still in jail at that time. But as far as I know, all war activities were halted in the second half of September, I believe. I was, of course, away from it all, but I think it was in September 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was this item of the agreement also later on included in the Dayton Accords and put into practice so as to affect the populations on all three war sides?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This item was implemented through the Dayton Accords. I think, however, that the return to Zepa began only as late as 2000. It all came about as a result of Dayton.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, towards the end, you spoke about Mr. Imamovic, Mr. Hajric, and the way they were taken from the prison where they were with you. Were they registered by the ICRC, like you were? Were they given an opportunity to get in touch with their families?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were registered the same day, and they also sent their messages to their families. Their families have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know who Mustafa Hodzic is? Was he imprisoned with you and did he participate in any military activities in Zepa? Was he in jail with you?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mustafa Hodzic. Well, the last name denotes a person from that area. But there were some 40 people there, and I cannot recall this name specifically. I don't remember him being with me in the prison. It could be one of the group, though, because I didn't know each and every person. I do not exclude that possibility. But he was never in the same cell with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Out of the 40 who were taken off the last bus, were they registered by the ICRC, were they all registered?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were all registered.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the interpreters, the witness, and the Presiding Judge, as well as the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is this: All those 40 people who were in Rogatica with you, were they registered by the ICRC and were they all later on exchanged, except for the two men whom you said were killed later on? And perhaps you can tell us when.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All 40, although I don't know whether it was a few less or more, with the exception of one person whose last name, I believe, was Cocalic, were registered. He was taken away from the jail, and his mortal remains were never found. Everyone else was registered by the ICRC and exchanged on the same day in January 1996 at Sarajevo Airport. Actually, first we were at Kula and then taken down to the center of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know who Mehan Oric is, son of Nezir? Was he from Zepa, and do you know anything about him? Was he with you in the jail in Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Oric is a Srebrenica family, the Orics, so he did not hail from Zepa. In any case, I don't recall him. Throughout my stay in the jail in Rogatica, I was in a separate room. For a while, I worked up at Borike, where there was a larger group of detainees, and this is when I slept with those people in the same room. However, all of the rest of the time at Rogatica, I was separated from the rest, and I saw other detainees at meal times.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know anything about Hamdija Dedic, son of Belaga [phoen]? Is he from Zepa? Do you have any information about him, and was he detained with you? Do you know whether he was killed during military activities in Zepa or subsequently as a detainee?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, Hamdija Dedic is the brother of a person who used to be a teacher in the elementary school in Zepa. I never saw him. But according to the statements of some people who were detained in Rogatica at the same time, he was captured. I think he was trying to reach Gorazde or Rudo, after which he was brought to the jail. He spent a few days at Rogatica. May I continue? And they say that he was taken away. It turned out he was killed, and I believe his mortal remains were recovered only a few years ago. He was subsequently buried in Zepa or Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When was he in prison? Was that during the events in Zepa or when you were there, and was he registered by the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you what I heard from other people. He arrived after the fall of Zepa, so in early August. He started from Rudo or Visegrad, in Eastern Bosnia, and ended up in Rogatica. That was in early August. He was not registered by the ICRC. He only spent a few days with us, and then he was taken away. As it turned out, he was subsequently killed, and I think his body was later on found in Vragolovi, in the general area of that location. In any case, I know he was later on buried, which happened a few years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. What do you know about Avdo Palic, from the point of his capture to his death, be it from what you heard from others or based on your own information?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my previous testimony, I said that the last time I saw Avdo Palic was on the morning of the 26th of July, 1995. I never saw him afterwards. There were things I heard, once I was released. These were stories or rumours, and I don't know if it's relevant to the Court. Allegedly, he was about to engage in some talks with the Serb side in the -- and that was on the 27th of July, together with one person escorting him. The Serb soldiers took him, and they told the escort to return. The person is still alive today. Following that, there was much discussion about the death of Avdo Palic among the Bosnian public. The latest version, if I may say, is the one that is generally considered to be true. It states that after being captured, he was held in the territory of the Rogatica municipality for a while, perhaps at Borike, and that he was later transferred to Batkovica, which was a camp close to Bijeljina in Northern Bosnia. Apparently in early September, he was returned to Rogatica or Han Pijesak, and it is presumed that he was killed at that time. This is how it was reported by journalists, and it is generally considered to be the truth, at least as far as the people in Sarajevo are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So you saw him for the last time on the 26th of July, when we returned from having escorted the first convoy, which left on the 25th. They travelled the whole night, crossing the lines. The same was repeated on the 27th, up until the last bus you mentioned. You know, at least according to the stories, that he was still alive in September?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were different theories about his fate, and that story developed for 10 years. What I'm telling you here is also not confirmed, but that figures as the latest and final version on the Bosnian side, at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell the Trial Chamber whether he was killed during combat operations, was he taken prisoner, or was he killed in the manner that you described just a moment ago in September?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can only repeat what I've already said. He certainly did not take part in any combat operations, and what I told you here were stories that journalists told and also what was related by his escort. Everything else is just conjecture. And, again, as I said, the latest valid truth -- version of the truth is that he was killed in early September 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether he was in the free territory of Republika Srpska on the 25th -- the night of the 25th, on the 26th, and the 26th and the 27th, when he accompanied the convoy, and that he even went to the separation line, to the positions held by the federation?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is what I know: I know that he was with you on the 25th, in the evening, and that he boarded a VRS vehicle, together with you, and you left. That is the last time I saw him, and it was already getting dark. He was supposed to accompany his family, and according to these stories, he did go to Kladanj. I don't know if he ever went to the lines held by the Federation Army. When he returned on the 26th, he told me that had briefly met with General Mladic at Boksanica on his way back and that Mladic had told him that I was supposed to go up there, as agreed earlier with Mladic, or, rather, as Mladic's earlier demand was, in order to guarantee for your security in Zepa, because as I've already said, the Army of Republika Srpska had not entered Zepa yet at that point in time. And that was, in fact, the last time that I saw Palic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now tell the Trial Chamber whether anyone was killed after being captured in the course of combat operations and during the transfer of the population by members of the VRS or those people who had organised the transfer of people from Zepa to Kladanj?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already answered this question on several occasions. I don't know exactly how many fighters or soldiers were killed in combat, itself. During the evacuation, no one was taken off the convoy except those 40 people, elderly men and wounded, who were taken off the last convoy. As I said, all of them, except one person, were later on exchanged in early 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any knowledge about anyone being taken off buses or being attacked by the civilians in Zepa? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, that did not happen, and I think I've said this clearly several times already.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, the reason I'm asking you is that there were also stories about people being raped and so on. Now, tell us, please, were you told and could you actually observe that all these activities were being filmed during the negotiations in Boksanica and the transfer?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I already answered and said that I did see all those events being filmed, but I wasn't going to say it then. But I did see the cameraman, and I knew that everything was being filmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We had occasion to see some of that footage here in the courtroom, and portions of those conversations that we could see and hear actually helped refresh our memory, and this was to assist the Trial Chamber. Would it be of even greater assistance if everything had been filmed? Would that have been more useful, both for the Trial Chamber or the Court and for us, that all the events, everything, absolutely everything, had been filmed?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the more information one has, the clearer the picture one has of any event.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I promised you that I would show you a video-clip from the Boksanica meeting, but then the Trial Chamber intervened and it wasn't necessary, and the Trial Chamber could see that there were -- that there was no pressure exerted of any sort on you. And if you feel that we need to show that video-clip, we can.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you now tell me whether the negotiators, and I won't mention their names, who were from Zepa and who negotiated with representatives of the VRS, had the mandate and the authority to negotiate and to put forward their proposals? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I will now speak about the 19th and the 24th of July. We had an agreement and the mandate to negotiate, but only in respect of the civilian population. And, again, I have to reiterate that the able-bodied or military-aged men were out of our competence. They were not -- we did not have the mandate for that, nor could anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the question that Ratko Mladic put, whether you were ready to negotiate, right at the outset of the meeting with him, and Kulovac said, Yes, when Mladic asked Kulovac whether he had the mandate and the authority to negotiate, and Kulovac answered in the affirmative, was that, in fact, so?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to be honest, I've tried to remember those moments, but it was difficult. And whether he had any previous agreement with Avdo without my knowledge, and whether he had any ideas or any thoughts in that respect, I don't know, but what I can confirm is that before we left off for the negotiations, Benjamin, Avdo, and I did not really talk about that, as far as I can recall, much less was any agreement or any arrangement agreed between us. And these people, I have to say, were very prominent people in Zepa, and they were an important factor in these events, and they could have an influence on the civilian population. But whether I was involved in any agreements about whether we should or shouldn't surrender the weapons, whether the able-bodied men should or shouldn't surrender the weapons, no, it did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But did the VRS put, as a condition for all the other negotiations, this one condition that able-bodied men should surrender their weapons? Was that a logical position on the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, from their point of view, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now, could we still consider an area a demilitarised area if soldiers are still armed?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the very term "demilitarisation" means that -- or implies that no weapons should be in the area, so that name, itself, tells you that the first thing that has to be done is that the weapons have to be removed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir, for your testimony. Thank you for your answers and for your fair conduct, and I wish you a safe trip and may God bless you in all your activities. And I would like to thank you and everyone else on behalf of the Defence, including the interpreters, the Technical Service, and the Trial Chamber for their assistance over the past eight days in carrying out these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Thayer, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I do, Mr. President. I thank you, and good morning to you and Your Honours. Good morning to the Defence. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Before I get going, and I just want to say this in open session - we don't need to go into private session - I just want to let you know again that I deeply and personally regret the discomfort, the insecurity, that you've expressed to the Trial Chamber. You don't need to respond. I just wanted you to understand my feelings about this matter, and I just feel obligated to let you know that. Let me pick up, sir, with some of the documents General Tolimir showed you most recently, and the first is 1D00267, the list that you had in hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is D111, marked for identification, just for --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes. I beg your pardon, Mr. President. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, General Tolimir yesterday tendered this list, he said, so as to reflect the fact, in his words, that there were no men of military age who were killed out of those on this list. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If my memory serves me well, General Tolimir, in reference to this list of names, said that this was the list of people who had left for Serbia. And I was asked to confirm whether these were local people from Zepa, based on the names that appear on the list, and that is what I answered and said. But from various reports and stories that people told me, I know what the fate of those people was, and everything that I said about this list was really based on hearsay, on what I heard others say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, either there was a misinterpretation of what I said or bad translation, but could Mr. Thayer please point the portion of the transcript where that was said, because I did not say that these were men of military age. I said these were men of military age who had crossed the mountain and went into Serbia because they didn't want to accept the proposal that they should disarm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I don't see any contradiction to the question of Mr. Thayer. But, Mr. Thayer, it would be really helpful if you could indicate where you are quoting from.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President. That's at transcript page 4791 to 4792, where the accused says: "Thank you, Mr. President. "I just seek to tender D267 into evidence so as to reflect the fact that there were no men of military age who were killed out of those on the list."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, do you know whether or not, with respect to the men on that list, the VRS was actually able to get its hands on them?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were questioned in Serbia by a VRS team, or, rather, this matter was investigated.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: That's another possible interpretation of what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was investigated in Serbia by a VRS team.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And my question to you is, sir: Do you have any knowledge about how these men and boys on this list that General Tolimir showed you made it over to Serbia? Do you know how they got there?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to reports that I heard, they crossed the Drina River, which was on the border of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Serbia, in that area. I don't have a lot of information about why they decided to do so. I don't know if there are any documents about that, but subsequently, I had occasion to talk to some of these people, and the answer was that because everyone was going, they went too. And some of them actually crossed over directly to the territory of Serbia and made their way through the territory under the control of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Trial Chamber anything that you learned about the circumstances of their crossing over, their leaving Zepa and crossing over to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I know is that after the 27th of July, all men of military age were in the area between the Zepa and Brlog mountains, which means that they were on the mountain plateau, and it is probable that they were still in communication with the General Staff of the BH Army at that time. Now, what happened afterwards, I really don't know, but basically they then dispersed and formed smaller groups that then moved through the territory under the control of Republika Srpska, and some of them crossed over into Serbia. How, or why, or where they got that idea from, I really don't know. I don't have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, did you ever hear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, just to clarify something, on page 16, lines 13 -- sorry, lines 13, 14, 15, it is recorded: "And some of them actually crossed over directly to the territory of Serbia and made their way through the territory under the control of the BH Army." Now, we heard, at the end of page 16: "I really don't know, but basically they then dispersed and formed smaller groups that then moved through the territory under the control of the Republika Srpska." I'm not sure if there is perhaps any contradiction. Perhaps you can clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, you're absolutely correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: These men and boys from Zepa -- describe to the Trial Chamber your understanding of the territories through which they passed and where they ended up. Just one more time so we have it clear on the transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is how it was: All men of military age from Zepa, and there were among them probably also those, as you suggested, who were young boys but who where afraid to board those buses lest they be taken off them, so they joined the other men, and generally they headed in two opposite directions. One group headed for Serbia, which was to the east. And the Zepa enclave has a direct border with Serbia at one point across the Drina River. That's on the east side of the enclave. And those are the men on this list. Now, the other group of men headed in the opposite direction. They headed westward or to the north-west, towards Kladanj, which was over or through the territory under the control of Serbs to the territory under the control of the BH Army. There were also groups, such as Hamdija Dedic's group that we mentioned a few moments ago, who headed towards Visegrad or Rogatica and so on. But most of them -- 95 per cent of them split and headed in these two directions that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, focusing for a minute on the men and boys who crossed the Drina River into Serbia, sir, can you share with the Trial Chamber anything you learned about the actual experience that they had as they made that crossing from Bosnia and Herzegovina, across the Drina River, to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, see, I only heard a few of those stories, so everything I'm going to tell you is really hearsay, it's based on stories told by others. But they were to the effect that it was really difficult, that they were afraid, and I assume that the best descriptions would be given by maybe a person who actually experienced that who could testify about it. But it was a long time ago, and I really don't know too many details.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, the Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, during my cross-examination, the witness -- I did not ask the witness about the structure, the composition, or anything else referring to the people from the list. I only asked if they were from the Zepa enclave and whether any of them were killed in the events surrounding Zepa in the period we are -- he was testifying about. We did not discuss either the sex or the age of these men or anything else. There was no mention made that there were children or anything to that effect. And if there was any such information, we need to be told about it in advance, because he can't ask -- you can't ask the Trial Chamber whether there were children or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, on the list, we can see the dates of birth, and maybe on the basis of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think you used this list by examination of this witness, and Mr. Thayer is allowed to do the same. I think it is not -- we can't follow your objection. Mr. Thayer, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Rest assured, sir, the Trial Chamber will hear from some of these men who, as you said, were fearful and swam across the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear that as these men were preparing to cross and as they crossed the river, that the VRS shot and shelled them as they fled across the river?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did hear stories to that effect. I don't know too many details, but one of the stories was to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, General Tolimir again, and this is at the transcript page 4773, suggested that these men and boys made it to Serbia, and I quote, "under the auspices of the ICRC." Now, we all know that once they reached Serbia, they were registered by the ICRC, but do you have any information that any of these men and boys who fled for their lives across the Drina River were in any way assisted by the ICRC before they did so?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. My knowledge was that after they were -- after they surrendered or were captured - I don't know what the best term is - by the Army of Yugoslavia, they were actually held and registered at two locations, Sljivovica and some field or other, and that that's where they were registered by the ICRC.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I never said that they had crossed the Drina under the auspices of the ICRC. There's either a transcript error or a translation error. What I did say was that later on they were registered by the ICRC. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, I provided the transcript cite for the Trial Chamber, and everybody can see what the general said.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: After these men from Zepa made it over to Serbia, in whose custody did they remain in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I know, and I'm probably not the best witness for that, but what I generally know, from the stories that were being told, was that they surrendered to the Army of Yugoslavia. And later on, at those two locations that I mentioned, they were questioned by teams of the VRS which arrived there. That's what I know, based on the stories of the people who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And based on those accounts from people with whom you've spoken and heard from, after those people were interviewed in Serbia by members of the VRS, did the VRS actually ever get their hands on any of the people on that list and bring them back to Bosnia or did they stay in Serbia after they were questioned by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I truly don't know that. Anything I'd say would amount to speculation. I don't exclude that possibility, but I'm really not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. We'll have other witnesses to testify about that, sir. Now, based on your knowledge, were all of these men and boys who fled over -- across the Drina River to Serbia soldiers or were some civilians as well?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably said something to that effect a moment ago. If I look at the list, I see a person who was, for example, born in 1976, which makes that person 19 years old. Other than that, I really don't know. I listened to what people had to tell me a full year later. I do not exclude the possibility of some civilians being with the group, and perhaps there were some people who were not able-bodied men or did not belong to that age category.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. You mentioned some boys who you said might have been too fearful to get on the buses. Let's look at this document, this list that General Tolimir showed you. And if we could go to page 8, please. Okay. Let's just focus on a couple of these entries. Do you see it on your screen, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We can see, as we're going across this chart, that we have the person's name, and then their date of birth, and what appears to be maybe their place of birth. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, place of birth.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And then there's a column that's headed "Pripadnost Jedinici." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should mean "Unit Membership," in other words, what military organisational unit they belonged to. In other words, it indicates whether a person was a member of the army or not. If they were, then the unit is specified. For example, I see here "The 1st Zepa Brigade." If we have a line, in the next column we are supposed to see their professions. And in most cases of the people who do not have any designation in the previous column, the last column states "Student."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at entry number 3. Do you see that, sir, on the far left column? These individuals are numbered, and it's number 3, but it's actually -- yeah, it's number 3, it looks like a "Sadet Muhic," date of birth --

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 16th of February, 1980. That's when he was born.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And we see, in the last column -- well, we see, in the last column, it says "Ucenik," and, again, what's that?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Ucenik" is a person attending a school. If I look at his date of birth, I'd say he was then in elementary school, in the eighth grade, according to Bosnian classifications. At that time, he was 15 years of age.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And as you mentioned a moment ago, that explains the line through the column for his military unit, indicating that, obviously, he doesn't have one; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely, and I explained that in detail, I believe, when I addressed the way these people were being put on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And if we just look a little further down the list, we can see similar lines and the designation of student at entry numbers 7, 8, 9, 11 and 12. Do you see that, sir, all of those entries with dates of birth in 1980 or 1978? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I did see it a moment ago when I commented on it. 7, 8, 9, 11 and 12, as well as 3 and 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, General Tolimir suggested to you that one of the reasons why all of these people on this list fled across the river was because they were afraid that they may have been on some kind of criminal indictment for the events that you talked about; combat or the ambush, however we want to characterise it, of 4 June 1992 at the Zlovrh elevation. Do you remember that question from General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, but I have a small correction to make. The clash took place a bit further away from Zlovrh, at Budicin Potok, and the aim of the military column that was attained was Zlovrh. Between Zlovrh, itself, and the place of the clash, there are between 10 and 15 kilometres, in my assessment. In any case, I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So all the people that we just talked about, these students, would have been, if I'm doing my math correctly, about 12 years old at that time, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, some even less. For example, this person was 10 years old -- no, sorry, 12. Most of them who were registered as students were of that age.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Given that there's no clear indication when they were 12, whether in 1992 or in 1995 when these activities took place, for the record, we should clarify when they were 12 and when they were older. We need to know how old they were at each point in time and how they were categorised under the law of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina as being fit for military service, or being part of the work force, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's a matter of simple arithmetic, and General Tolimir very well knows what this list shows and what these dates of birth are. He can look at the dates, just as we did, and do the math.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This was compiled in 1995, as we can see at the top of the -- on the 2nd of August, 1995, if I read it correctly. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, at the transcript page 4789 -- again, in the same way that General Tolimir showed you this list to suggest that men weren't killed by the VRS after they were captured, at 4789 of yesterday's transcript he asked you, and I quote: "Were there any able-bodied men killed by the VRS after they surrendered, with the exclusion of Avdo Palic, Amir Imamovic?" And then you added Mehmed Hajric later on. Do you remember that, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, Mr. Tolimir raised one topic, the age in Bosnia-Herzegovina -- in which age is a male person fit for military service. Could you please ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, did you understand the Presiding Judge's question?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand Mr. President's question in the following way: I would need to say how old a person has to be to be considered of military age under the then legislation in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The age is 18. One has to have celebrated his 18th birthday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, again, General Tolimir asked you this question yesterday at transcript page 4789: "Were there any able-bodied men killed by the VRS after they surrendered, with the exclusion of Avdo Palic, Amir Imamovic?" And then you added "Mehmed Hajric." Do you remember that question? He asked it, again, in relation, like he did with this list, to suggest that no men from Zepa were killed by the VRS.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. May we have 65 ter 202, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: As you can see, what we have here is a daily combat report from Lieutenant-Colonel Rajko Kusic, who you've numerous times identified as the commander of the Rogatica Brigade. It's dated the 8th of August, 1995. And paragraph 1, he writes and reports: "On 7 August 1995, in the afternoon, in the canyon of the Praca River ..." Just generally speaking, where is -- do you have any idea where this location would be, this canyon of the Praca River? We don't need GPS coordinates, but if you could just orient the Trial Chamber a little bit to where the canyon of the Praca River would be.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is to the south of Zepa, relatively close to Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Colonel Kusic continues: "Five remaining balijas, who were, after the fall of Zepa, travelling along the following route ..." And he gives the route here: "Luka, crossed the Drina River by boat, Kamenici Potok, Babina Gora, Gradina, Kapetanovici, crossed the Drina River on the logs, Crni Vrh, Kopito, above Medjedja, Ustipraca, went down to the railroad tracks at Dub and tried to reach Renovica, walking on the railroad tracks, were liquidated. "The group was separate and it travelled for 10 days." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: "The same day, in the vicinity of Luke, an unarmed Ustasha ..." Now, first of all, can you tell us, generally speaking, where Luke is?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Luke is north of Zepa. Administratively speaking, it was within the municipality of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It continues: "... in the vicinity of Luka, an unarmed Ustasha ..." Can you explain what this term "Ustasha" refers to here in Colonel Kusic's report?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Originally, Ustashas were members of the Croatian forces during the Second World War, allied with the fascists. During this war, it was used as a derogatory term by the Serbs to denote -- to designate membership in the Croatian forces and occasionally also in the Muslim forces. Perhaps I should correct myself. They also sometimes referred in that way to the members of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I should not have said "the Muslim forces."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, he continues: "... an unarmed Muslim," shall we say, "born in Srebrenica, 24 years old, was liquidated. Before he died, he said that he fell behind the others and he was looking for food." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, can you tell the Trial Chamber how this report of a hungry, unarmed Muslim male being liquidated by VRS forces as he travelled alone -- how does that correspond or not with this state of mind that you've told the Trial Chamber so many times about, this fear that you've described being possessed by the people of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a clear illustration of the fear. They were fearful of being killed without due process, without ever being able to say anything. If I may, I'd like to add something with regards to my yesterday's answers, when I answered the questions of Mr. Tolimir. I think his question was a bit more narrow. I can testify to what I know. For example, after the fall of Zepa, I think there was a witness testifying to that, saying something I also am aware of, those Zepa fighters who were captured by the VRS, as far as I know, according to the stories, there were 12 to 14 of them who were killed, and this person could be one of that group. I don't know why, but I guess that group was trying to reach Gorazde. Most of them were killed immediately. There was one case when a person was captured by the Visegrad Brigade. It was Dedija Hamdic [as interpreted], the person General Tolimir asked me about, and then there were some other cases of people from the municipality of Han Pijesak. So I don't want the record to reflect that no one was killed, but as far as I know, as far as I could hear, there were between 12 and 14 people who were killed following their capture.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, in the beginning of his cross-examination of you this morning, sir, General Tolimir asked you about some names. He put some names to you and asked you whether you knew some of these people. He asked you about a Selvir -- I'm sorry, a Mustafa Hodzic. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember the question. My answer was that I don't know who the person was, at least not off the top of my head. If my memory was refreshed, perhaps I might. I also subsequently recalled the Defence exhibit entitled "State Secret," and that Samir Halilovic is the son of General Halilovic. And I also recall that the title of his book was "State Secret," and I needed a document to jog my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. May we go into private session for a couple of questions, please, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I see we're at the break, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Exactly. We are now at the time for the first break. We adjourn, and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just to let the Trial Chamber know, I furnished the Defence the information that formed the basis of my additional question concerning Mr. Mustafa or Mujo Hodzic. And I don't mean to be cagey or cryptic, it's just that our practice is to try to not let what one witness -- while one witness is here, let what another witness said possibly influence their testimony. So we don't like the cross-pollination potential, so we try to keep our witness's testimony based, as much as possible, on their own experience. And that's the only reason why I preferred to do that out of the hearing of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I understand your intention. On the other hand, we should be able to follow and to understand what is the basis for some question. That was the reason why we asked you to provide us with this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And I can hand up -- if the Court wishes to see the actual document, I have an additional copy, and I can hand that up to the Trial Chamber just to see what I was talking about or where the question emanated from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It depends on the question how you intend to proceed with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That water is long under the bridge. I've moved on from that set of questions. And his knowledge, as you saw, about that particular individual was nil, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's right. Please, just move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. President. At this time, the Prosecution would tender 65 ter 202.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P755.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, just to follow up with a final question on this general topic: You referred to Mr. Palic at some point being accompanied by an escort, and you indicated that that person is still alive. Do you know the name of that person, and can you share it?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know for a fact that he's still alive. But what his name is, I can't really recall. I can see his face before me, but I can't recall his name. I'm sorry. If you help me, give me a cue of some sort, I might be able to remember it. I know who you are referring to. I know that he is still alive. His last name might be Piric, but I don't really want to guess. He is a young man, much younger than me. And as I said, I can see him before me, but I just can't recall the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what was his position, his unit, if you know?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What unit? Well, he was someone who was an aide to Colonel Palic, as it were. He was a soldier who always went with him. I think he was from Avdo's village, from Krivaca, most probably, from the same village where Avdo was from.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. What I want to do now, sir, is just go back to some specific portions of your testimony and ask you some follow-up questions. Back on the 30th of August, and this was at transcript page 4568, you were testifying about the order that Colonel Palic received to conduct some operations, and that members of the War Presidency disagreed with that order. Do you remember those questions being asked of you, both in your examination-in-chief and in cross-examination, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember it, but I think the date was not the 30th of August. It must have been something else, because it's impossible. The 30th of August, Zepa had already fallen. Maybe it was misinterpreted.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I meant that the 30th of August was the date of your testimony here. I was just --

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- for the record. Let me just quote back to you this question and answer, and I just want to ask a follow-up question. General Tolimir asked you, and again this is at transcript page 4568 on 30 August: "During the examination-in-chief, you said that the War Presidency was against attacks being launched from within the enclaves?" And your answer was: "Yes." You were asked: "Tell us a little bit more about that." And then you answered: "Well, that was a reference to an order that had arrived, and I think I was shown that order three and a half years ago, when I testified here. I think it was a Defence exhibit. It referred to the period of June 1995, and I think that the situation was that the situation was worsened at the time. We received this order from the War Presidency, and Avdo Palic actually did these things, although we were against it." Okay. Have you had a chance to have that translated to you? And, first, I see you have something to say, and that may actually get to my next question, so go ahead.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember this, but I don't remember saying we received this order from the War Presidency. Maybe it was misinterpreted. It doesn't make sense. And then Avdo Palic -- in other words, this order could have come - that's what I said - from some command, whether from the 2nd Corps or some other part of the BH Army, so it's a bit unclear to me, this portion of the transcript which begins with: "We received this order from ...," and then onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, because that was the question I had, was whether your testimony was, in fact, that this military order came from the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know how that found its way here, but that order had come from the BH Army Command, I think from the Command of the 2nd Corps specifically, because the 28th Division was officially under their command. And then, lower down, we had the 285th Brigade of that division, and so this is what struck me as different, and that is why I reacted. This order did not come from the War Presidency or any other political body.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, at transcript page 4285, and this was from the 23rd of August, 2010, you testified that from spring 1993 until spring 1995, and I quote: "During that period, as far as I can remember, there was occasional shelling, but there were no infantry attacks against the Zepa enclave. I believe that the shelling in question always came in response to some of the events outside of the Zepa enclave." And then you added at the next page that, I quote: "I meant to say that they were probably retaliating for something." And you further recalled, I quote: "I think once they targeted the center of Zepa, speaking from memory, I believe it was in response of the VRS to NATO bombardment of certain targets at Jahorina. I think I can tie these two things together." And you added that it was possible this was in May of 1995. Do you recall that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And do you recall whether any safe areas, other than the Zepa enclave, were shelled by the VRS that same day, whatever day it was in May?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall, as I sit here. But it would make sense, if these things were connected, that all the enclaves should be shelled. When I say "all," I mean Srebrenica and Gorazde to the south. But whether it actually did happen, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And in a minute I'm going to get to the crux of my question, which goes to a document that General Tolimir showed you, and we'll look at that document in a second and you'll see why I'm trying to lay this foundation for you. The next document I want to show you, before going back to General Tolimir's document, is 65 ter 6020, please. We'll just briefly look at this cover page before we go into the document, itself. What we have here is it's an UNPROFOR document from the Civil Affairs officer from the UNPROFOR Command, and it's dated 7 June 1995, concerning -- what it says here is "the Tuzla incident." And if we can go to the second page, please, and this is what I want to focus on. It says here at the heading "Shelling of Tuzla Air Force Base and Tuzla Old Town, 25 May 1995." And we do have a B/C/S translation of this document which should be available in e-court. If not, I'll just continue reading the relevant section. It says: "As a sequel to air-strikes administered by NATO at Pale Ammo Dump, BSA," that's the term they used for the VRS at the time, "resorted to massive retaliatory artillery shelling against Tuzla Town and Tuzla Air Force Base, which is considered deliberate targeting of UN troops and Tuzla Safe Area ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, we have it on the screen now, the B/C/S translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you very much, Mr. President, and it's the first paragraph in both versions we're looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And it refers to a number of shells, and one of them hitting the old part of Tuzla city center, a place where young people flock together. And as a consequence, 66 people were massacred and 170 wounded, 31 critically. Now, the reason I'm asking you about this document is: First of all, do you recall this incident happening at the time?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, that's a matter that was well known to everyone in Bosnia. That happened on the 25th of May, and every year this event is marked, when a shell killed 66 people, most of them young people, because it was a place where young people gathered aged between 15 and 25, let's say. And as far as I can recall, that happened in the afternoon/early evening hours. And I think that this case was prosecuted at local -- before the local court in Sarajevo, and I don't know if some sentences were passed to officers who are responsible for this shelling. So this is a well-known incident. It can be compared to Markale and other incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We should know whether this is what the witness recollects from that period and whether the shelling was executed by the commander of the Drina Corps, which was in charge of combat activities around Zepa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, would you follow up?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, do you have any idea of which unit of the VRS was responsible for this shelling?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know is that the shell arrived from the Serb positions at Majevica, which is a mountain. It is to the north-east of the center of Tuzla. I don't know what the actual areas of responsibility between the corps of the VRS was. I don't know whether it was the Drina Corps or not. What I do know and what I could read was that the shell had come from a position at Majevica. I don't know what corps there was. Perhaps it could be found in some documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And my question is actually very simple, sir, and it is this: Having your recollection refreshed about the date of this incident, which you've told us everybody in Bosnia knows about, does that help you place the date of the shelling that you described and that I read back to you from your testimony, which you said was possibly in May of 1995 and that you thought was in response to NATO bombardment of certain targets at Jahorina? So, again, my question is just very simple. Is there any relationship between the dates of the Tuzla shelling and the shelling that you recalled and testified about occurring sometime in May? Just try to see if that jogs your recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you answer. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Since we are relying here on the witness's recollection, and the witness is referring to proceedings before national courts, perhaps he should be asked whether anyone from the firing position of Ozren was sentenced for that crime and whether Majevica was in the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps as well as Ozren.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tolimir, but this is a recommendation for Mr. Thayer. But at the moment, Mr. Thayer is putting questions to the witness, and I think he should carry on. Witness, do you recall the question of Mr. Thayer? If that is the case, please provide us with an answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do remember it. The shelling of the center of Zepa happened in late May. The event in Tuzla took place on the 25th of May. Following that logic, one would say that it all happened around the same date. If I may, I'd like to respond briefly to Mr. Tolimir's intervention. I did say "Majevica," but it was most likely from Ozren, which is on the opposite side. I don't know who the person who was sentenced for it was. In any case, Majevica or Ozren doesn't mean much to me. They were both positions in existence at the time. It could well be that it was Ozren, but Ozren is on the opposite side, so we're speaking about the north-easterly and north-westerly direction. In any case, it was all around the 25th of that month.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we could take a look at D98, which is the document that General Tolimir showed you and which is the reason I'm asking you all of these questions to begin with. If we could have that up on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: While we're getting this enlarged in English, just to bring you back a little bit: General Tolimir showed this to you at transcript page 4584, and that was on the 30th of August, and we can see here again it's a report by Avdo Palic and it's dated the 28th of May, 1995. And my question for you emanates from General Tolimir's question to you in his cross-examination. He asked you if you knew anything about why the measures were taken that are described in here, and again we have here at item 1: "Measures have been taken to seal off the areas controlled by UNPROFOR and the direction of possible withdrawal. "No signs were registered of the situation deteriorating or anything that would indicate a possible withdrawal of UNPROFOR, except for their fear, to an extent, of a possible Chetnik attack." Now, again, General Tolimir asked you whether you know anything about why these measures were taken at the time. And having had your recollection refreshed about the shelling of the Tuzla Air Force Base, and the targeting of UNPROFOR, and, to use the words in that document, the massacre of those civilians, can you enlighten the Trial Chamber any further than you were able to a few days ago, having had your recollection refreshed now about the dates of these events? Is there any connection? If there isn't, please let us know. If there is, please let us know, sir.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I can. I remember it as a particularly heavy shelling of the center of Zepa, when the mosque was hit as well. That was in the very center of Zepa. Some 10 shells landed. At that point in time, it was expected that an infantry attack would ensue against the enclave. Avdo seems to be referring to a document of the 26th of May, whereas this one is of the 28th of May, so they were probably in communication about what to do. He reported on the measures undertaken. This is what it is about, I believe. I remember the shelling, in any case, and I remember it was on a Friday, because on that day the Muslims follow a specific religious ritual.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you remember at this time, following this NATO air attack, various UN peacekeepers being taken hostage and chained to various potential NATO targets? Do you remember that happening at the time as well, sir?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I think that footage was shown on Serb TV and radio. Everyone in Bosnia is familiar with that. It's a widely-known story. I remember the footage very well. There seemed to have been a soldier tied to a pole on top of a hill. It was a soldier from one of the countries of the West, I believe. He may well have been a Dutch soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I think we're finished with that topic, and the Prosecution would tender 65 ter 6020, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P756.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Jumping around just a little bit, sir, at transcript page 4614 to 4615 you made some reference to wealthy inhabitants of Zepa. That term can mean vastly different things, depending on where you are and the time-period. Can you just tell the Trial Chamber, when you refer to wealthy inhabitants of Zepa, what are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I please see the transcript so that I could look into the context? Even a sentence would help me. I believe General Tolimir's question was about one of his documents or, rather, one of the documents of the Defence, where it said that a part of the population of Zepa, some well-off citizens wished to leave Zepa for some third countries. I have a hazy recollection of that. But if you can't give me any further context, I can try to speak from memory and explain what I meant by wealthy or well-off inhabitants. Well, I'd say that those who were well off were those who could meet their necessities in order to survive at the time, who had some of the things most of which were hard to get. People were happy to have flour, oil, salt and sugar, these basic necessities which could secure your survival. In Zepa, even before the war, there weren't people who were particularly well off. Most of them were farmers, so we can't talk about any wealth in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Just another point for clarification. At transcript page 4722, you referred to a meeting with Alija Izetbegovic, and my question is simply: Did you actually have any face-to-face meetings with President Izetbegovic in July of 1995, or ever, or is that a problem with the transcript or some other problem?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, in July 1995 -- well, it was probably recorded wrongly. We had those discussions with Mr. Izetbegovic. There were no meetings, of course, with him. I either misspoke or was misinterpreted. In any case, we used radio communication. I did meet Mr. Izetbegovic, as a member of a delegation from Zepa. There were also delegations from Srebrenica and Gorazde. I think it took place in September 1993 in Sarajevo. We were visiting. There were between eight and ten of us from Zepa, and we had a short meeting with Mr. Izetbegovic. It was in September 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. No big deal, sir. I just wanted to clarify that one transcript page. Now, what I'd like to do for the next few minutes is ask you some questions about the meeting you had on the 13th of July with General Tolimir at Boksanica. There was a question from the Honourable Judge Mindua about the meeting and a document that General Tolimir showed you in his cross-examination, and I'm not sure if you answered the question. General Tolimir, at page 4309, said that you misinterpreted his words at the meeting. So what I want to do is just take a little bit of time and ask you, again, some foundational questions, show you a couple of documents, and then I'm going to take another crack at Judge Mindua's question and see where we are. Okay? And Ms. Stewart will assist us with putting up some transcript pages. First, and I don't know we need to see the actual transcript right now because it was pretty recent -- well, actually, you know what? Let me go back. Do you recall being asked in the Popovic case to describe the 13 July meeting with General Tolimir, which was attended by yourself and Mujo Imamovic? Do you remember being asked about that?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall what your answer was? And, again, if you want to see the transcript, Ms. Stewart is certainly able to put that up for you, and it's from 30 March 2007.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. When I testified then is what I can remember. At that meeting with General Tolimir, we were told that Srebrenica had fallen and that it was Zepa's turn next. This could be dealt with in two ways. The peaceful way, by evacuating the entire population. And I followed it up by my question whereby I asked whether a 35-year-old man could leave, and the answer I received from General Tolimir was, Yes, of course. Next, he said that if he didn't accept that possibility, there would be a military invasion on Zepa. This is what I can recall from that conversation. Regarding the rest of my testimony and the answer to General Tolimir's question, I believe some things may have remained unclear.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let me just stop you there --

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- and ask you if you remember being asked essentially the same question in 1998, during your OTP interview in January of 1998. Do you recall being asked the same question, and do you recall what you told the investigators then about the meeting? And, again, if you need to take a look at your statement, we can certainly put that up.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that. I don't need to see the statement. What I just said a moment ago is what should be reflected in the statement; perhaps not word for word, but the gist of it is definitely the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's just take a look at D109 very quickly. It's your statement. General Tolimir showed you a lot of it during your testimony. It's page 6 of the English, and it will be the bottom of page 5 in the B/C/S. And we shouldn't broadcast this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And we're looking at the bottom paragraph of the B/C/S, and it's the top paragraph of the English. Do you see where it says: "Tolimir did all the talking, he said that we could do this in two ways. First, he wanted a complete evacuation of the whole population. I asked Tolimir if a 35-year-old man could leave by just climbing on the bus. He replied, 'Of course.' Should we refuse the first way, then military action would follow." Now, my question is: You go on in this statement to say that: "He suggested that we should start the evacuation immediately and that they would bring the buses. Tolimir stated that the evacuation should take place in the same way that it had taken place in Srebrenica." My question is simple, sir. We obviously see that your recollection of this has remained constant. My specific question, in looking at this, is: Do you recall him suggesting that the evacuation should start immediately, and that they would bring the buses, and that the evacuation would be handled the same way as in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, I gave this statement in 1998, I believe. We were much closer to the events then than we are now. From this position here, I can't fall back on anything more than what I had already said that may be in my memory. This is 12 years later, and I'm afraid I can't say anything in addition to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Understood, sir. I guess the question is, then, two questions. Do you have any reason to doubt the accuracy of what's here in your witness statement? Do you stand by this additional portion of your statement that I just read to you?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can repeat what I said already. Back in 1998, that is what I could recall. It was also further discussed when Mr. Tolimir examined and some other documents were shown. 1998 was only three years after the events. This is what I said then, and I stand by each and every of my statements. Perhaps there may be a few corrections that could be made anywhere, but I always said -- told the truth and to the best of my recollection. I stand by each of my statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So just to clarify, the ultimatum, as you described it in your testimony, that General Tolimir gave you on the 13th of July, complete evacuation of the entire population or military action, that ultimatum, can you help us in terms of when, during this meeting, that ultimatum came? Did it come at the beginning, for example, the middle, or the end?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it came at the very beginning, as far as I recall, at the beginning of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And that brings us to the Honourable Judge Mindua's question, which I think you've already touched on just recently. If we could look at P491. This is this report that you referred to, that General Tolimir showed you during your cross-examination. And if we can go to page 2 of the English. There were these five items that are described here, and I won't go back through all your testimony about it, but Judge Mindua had specific questions regarded to item 5, for example, which indicates the requests of the Zepa representatives at this meeting to enable them to stay in the territory, for the persons who choose to do so. My question, again, is very simple. These five items, were they discussed before or after General Tolimir issued you the ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely after that, speaking from memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, at transcript page 4689, General Tolimir suggested in his question that the Muslims from Zepa interrupted the talks between the 13th and the 19th of July. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what happened after you didn't show up or didn't provide the response they were looking for on the 14th of July? So what happened between the evening of the 13th of July and 19 July?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, and I believe I said that a few times during my testimony, on the 13th, in the evening, military attacks were launched on Zepa. All contact ceased. There was no further communication with the Serb side, and we organised our lines of defence. Those military attacks against Zepa lasted until the 19th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And then after your meeting on the 19th of July at Boksanica with General Tolimir and General Mladic, what happened, when nobody from Zepa showed up to be removed on the 20th of July, until the 24th of July, when you were summoned to Boksanica again?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave evidence on that, too. The attacks on Zepa resumed between the 20th and the 24th, and I think I mentioned at some point that those attacks were far heavier than they had been before.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, General Tolimir also referred in his cross-examination to various meetings and conversations involving an individual named David Harland. Just for your information, if you don't know who he is, he was an UNPROFOR member who was a Civil Affairs officer. And General Tolimir showed you some documents and excerpts of things that referred to various meetings with David Harland, and I want to show you a couple of reports that concern the events between the 19th of July, after your meeting, when you said you expected there to be talks at the airport to help resolve this "all for all" exchange issue, and the 24th of July, when you were brought back to Boksanica. And I want to ask you about just a couple of paragraphs from these reports and see how they correspond or not to what was going on on the ground. The first one I want to look at, please, is 65 ter 2076. We can see that this is dated 20 July 1995, and its subject is "Negotiations on Zepa." It's an UNPROFOR report from David Harland. What I want to do is go to page 2 of the English, please, and that will be page 3 of the B/C/S, where Mr. Harland provides an assessment. And I'd like you to take a moment and read this assessment, and tell the Trial Chamber to what extent this assessment reflects the events on the ground, as you were experiencing them, as you understood them at the time.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you just clarify this last portion, where it says: "Who is it who does not have any particular interest in --" I think there's some problem with the translation. It's all right now. I understand. Sarajevo does not see any particular interest. Well, I would agree with the better part of this assessment by this gentleman. I don't recall his name.
