utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's just take it a little chunk at a time. Do you agree with his assessment that the Serbs do not want to make a final infantry assault on Zepa, due to the nature of the terrain, wherein there would inevitably be substantial casualties?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that assessment was correct, and that was in evidence because you could see how Serbs actually took control of Zepa part by part, and then there would be a break, and then the negotiations would continue. So I would agree with his assessment as regards the final infantry assault on Zepa because, as far as I know and what I learned from some Serb soldiers while I was imprisoned, they generally were anxious about these infantry assaults on Zepa because of the terrain and because of the negative experience they had with it in 1992. Other than that attempt, there were some other attempts that we mentioned, and some we didn't, where the Serb forces did not manage to get through and they had casualties. This was the reason why their approach was as we see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And Mr. Harland refers to: "Their approach will be bombard and negotiate." Do you agree with that assessment or disagree with that assessment?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm trying to think of what I should say now. But as I analyse this, basically, that's how the entire story with Zepa actually developed. There were one, two, three negotiations that I took part in, and then there were attacks preceding each one of those, most of them shelling, in fact. Bombing and shelling in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would tender 65 ter 2076, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P757.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. To save some time, I'll skip one of these reports. May we have 65 ter 2438, please. And we'll need to go to page 25 of this document, please. Unfortunately, we don't have a B/C/S translation, but the portion we'll be discussing is very short, so I can just read that portion to the witness. And if we could go to the next page, please. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We have here another report from David Harland. This one is dated the 22nd of July, and it just says that it attaches a memo on the subject. And if we could just go to the next page, please. We see, again, the date of this report is 22 July. Its subject is "Negotiations on Zepa, number 4." And if we could go to the next page, and again we'll be focusing on the assessment. And I just want to get your assessment of the assessment. It's --

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we have the translation, please? I need the translation. I can't -- I don't read English.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, unfortunately, we don't have a translation of this paragraph, or this document, but I'll just read it into the record for you and it will be translated that way. Okay? It's under the heading "Assessment," and it starts out: "Our proposal for the total demilitarisation of Zepa remains a long shot. It is true that the Serbs are reluctant to attack the Zepa pocket until they have completely worn down its population. On the other hand, it is hard to imagine that they would accept any arrangement that would leave Zepa in Bosnian hands. I imagine that they will continue to make life in Zepa as miserable as possible for the local population until, demoralised by the assault and abandoned by the international community, they accept the 'evacuation' option being proposed by the Serbs. "Our chances of success are small, but we will continue with the initiative until it is definitely rejected by the Serbs." Again, can you tell the Trial Chamber how this corresponds or not, in terms of its description, to what you were experiencing on the ground at the time?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, it does correspond, for the most part, to my experience. The entire situation in those two years and the developments toward the end were such that I can agree with this assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: In case the Trial Chamber is wondering, I'll reserve tendering this document because it actually is a collection of reports that came in in the last case with one 65 ter number as a collection. So I don't know if that makes life difficult for Registry, but I will not be tendering that until we offer the entire packet through another witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And taking into account the amount of pages, I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you just told us a little while ago about the continuous shelling from the 13th through the 19th, and then the 20th through the 24th as it intensified. You told us that by the 24th of July, in your words, I think, that the population was near panic. And you also talked about -- early in your testimony about the vulnerable situation that the civilian population found itself in as it had fled to the Zepa Mountain. Now, General Tolimir referred, in a number of his questions, to the VRS preferring peaceful options and wanting to avoid a fight, and that's at transcript pages 4747 and 4777. I want to show you a document and again ask you about a certain part of it to see how it corresponds to your state of mind and the state of mind of the population in Zepa at the time. Can we see P488, please. What we have here, sir, is a report and proposal from General Tolimir to the Main Staff of the VRS. It's dated 21 July 1995. As you can see, it's headed "Situation in Zepa." I don't think you've ever been shown this document before, but I'd ask you just to take a few moments and read through it, and then I have some specific questions about certain portions of it.

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I want to focus your attention on paragraphs 4 and 5. I'm sorry, if we can go back, in the English, to paragraph 4 on the prior page. Just paragraph 4, please. Thank you. It says: "We believe that we would be in more advantageous position for direct negotiations after we inflict losses on enemy's military personnel. We request means for crashing enemy's defence in the areas of Brezova Ravan and Purtici." If we can go to the next page, which is paragraph 5: "The most propitious means of their destruction would be usage of chemical weapons or aerosol grenades and bombs. Using these means would accelerate the surrender of Muslims and the fall of Zepa. "We will continue with combat activities using weapons for direct targeting in order to penetrate into the above-mentioned axes." And then, finally, General Tolimir writes: "We believe that we could force Muslims to surrender sooner if we would destroy groups of Muslim refugees fleeing in the direction of Stublic, Radava, and Brloska Planina." Now, this proposal from General Tolimir to the Main Staff to destroy groups of Muslim refugees, can you tell the Trial Chamber how this type of proposal, what you see here, corresponds or not corresponds to the fear that you described permeating this entire period in July 1995 with respect, in particular, to the civilian population and its fate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This document that was -- that is quoted shows that I did not ask for the destruction of the civilian population, but, rather, refugees and not the civilian population, and in the direction of Stublic, Radava, Brloska Planina, and I would appreciate it if the questions put are in keeping with this, with what is stated therein.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, can you answer my question, looking at the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please think about to change a little bit the wording of your question. That was the request of Mr. Tolimir. In particular, to the civilian population, that is his problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, sir, you can read that last paragraph in your own language. Can you answer my question, whether that corresponded or had any correspondence/correlation to the fear that you were telling the Trial Chamber about, what is proposed here by General Tolimir in this document?

utterances.speaker: HAMDIJA TORLAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I've read the entire document, and this is exactly reflective of the fear that I mentioned and repeatedly spoke about during my evidence here, the fear that the population there had, and this, in fact -- this corresponds to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Witness, I have no further questions. I thank you for your endurance and your patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, first of all, the Chamber would like to thank you for your patience, for your attendance here at the trial, and for the way you were able to assist the Chamber and to provide answers for all the questions put to you during exactly two weeks. We are really very grateful and hope you will be able to relax after these two very difficult weeks for you. This concludes the questioning for you. The Chamber would like to thank you again and wishes you all the best for your future. Now you may return to your normal activities. I think the next witness will be ready for examination. We should have the second break now. It gives us the opportunity to arrange everything that has to be arranged. And we will adjourn now and resume a quarter before 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before the witness should be brought in, I would like to mention two matters. The first one is in relation to our decision about presentation of evidence, especially regarding the accused's compliance with paragraph 1 of that decision, which requires that within seven days of receiving the Prosecution's list of witnesses it intends to call during the following calender month, the accused is to provide the Chamber and the Prosecution with its estimate of the time required for cross-examination for each witness. The Chamber has yet to received any such list and would very much appreciate the accused's compliance therewith. This was to enable the other party to prepare the examination of that witness. My second remark is addressed to the Prosecution. We have realised that there are some exhibits proposed to use with the witness which are not yet in the 65 ter exhibit list. When the Prosecution seeks to use a document whose 65 ter number is greater than 6184 [Realtime transcript read in error "6584"] - that's the end of the 65 ter exhibit list - we would like to ask the Prosecution to move for an addition of the document to the 65 ter exhibit list. And if that is the case, we would like to ask the accused if there is any objection to that. That's just a remark which should be taken into account. And I'm not sure about that, but I formed the impression that some of the exhibits the Prosecution wants to use with the next witness are not yet on that list. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, good afternoon. As regards your first remark, I want to say the following: This Defence is trying to offer as good an estimate as possible we need for cross-examination, and I believe so far our estimates were quite realistic. We even managed to take less time in some cases. As regards the upcoming witnesses, during the day tomorrow we will be sending a list which can be relied on by the OTP, the Chamber, and the Registrar. Any delay in producing the list was the result of our willingness to provide as best information as possible to all the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. Gajic, we noticed that the cross-examination was, with very few exceptions, always within the time-limit you indicated in advance. Thank you for that. Mr. Thayer, is there, related to the second question, anything to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be better if I liaised with the Court Officers instead of taking up court time. But I do have some questions about the Court's instruction, but I'll just do it another way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We agree, and the witness should be brought in, please. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the Registrar and the Chamber to bear in mind that I kindly requested that we work on Mondays in the afternoon, or on other days, because that time is required for me to consult with my legal representatives. And this month, for example, we worked on Mondays three times already. That was one thing. Another thing: For example, we sat yesterday evening, and today we were sitting in the morning. I am brought in to my cell just before the lights go out, and I don't even have time to go and get the documents I needed from my working room. And the next morning, I have to leave as early as quarter to 7.00. Therefore, there is no time whatever left for my preparation. Please bear in mind that I need time for preparation, at least half an hour a day as the minimum. Once we concluded the session here, I arrived in my cell very late, and in the mornings I'm here at 7.30 already. If the Registrar has any influence over this, could please this be borne in mind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we understand your request, and it is always a very difficult procedure to find the right way how to schedule the hearings. There are so many different interests we should put together to find a solution which is convenient for everybody. But we will consider your request again, and thank you for this submission. Sorry for that delay. Sir, welcome to the Tribunal. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Would you please read the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I suppose Mr. Thayer has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Would you please state your name for the record?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB
utterances.text: It's Thomas Neason Dibb.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall testifying here over the course of three days in October 2007?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you recently have an opportunity to review your testimony in that case, the Popovic case?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Kindly observe a pause between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apologies, Your Honour. It seems that the name of the witness was recorded incorrectly at page 63, line 15 -- line 10, I'm sorry. So page 63, line 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Indeed, it is wrong. It will be corrected. Please carry on, Mr. Thayer. And now you are in the same position as Mr. Tolimir at other instances quite often. Please pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, can you attest before this Trial Chamber that the testimony which you read accurately reflects what you said in that prior trial?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB
utterances.text: Yes, it did, it accurately reflected that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you attest before this Trial Chamber that were you asked the same questions today that you were asked back in October 2007, that your answers would be the same?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB
utterances.text: Yes, they would.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution would tender P741, the witness's testimony in the Popovic case, none of which is under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received as P741.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I'll proceed to read the Rule 92 ter summary and then tender the associated exhibits afterwards. The witness was born and raised in Zimbabwe, then joined the British Army in 1991. He studied Serbo-Croatian at the army language school, and as a lieutenant served as a liaison officer and interpreter at Gornji Vakuf from November 1993 until May of 1994. In the spring of 1994, he and a colleague were injured by a mine that killed another officer, so he returned to the UK, whereafter he served with his battalion in Northern Ireland until November 1994. In January 1995, he completed a refresher language course, then deployed to UNPROFOR's BiH Command in Sarajevo as a captain in April 1995, serving as an interpreter and liaison officer primarily to the Serb side. He left the army in early 1996 to work for the Halo Trust, an international de-mining organisation, and served in Mozambique, Republic of Georgia, Chechnya, Kosovo, Sri Lanka, Cambodia, South Lebanon, and most recently Afghanistan. On the Serb military side, his main contact was Colonel Indjic, who was based in the Lukavica Barracks in Sarajevo. On the civilian side, his contact was an aide to President Karadzic named Jovan Zametica. Captain Emma Bliss served as a liaison officer and interpreter dealing primarily with the Bosniak side. On 14 July 1995, General Nicolai's deputy chief of staff, Colonel Coiffet, was sent to Tuzla to report directly back to BiH Command about the situation of the refugees arriving from Srebrenica. The witness accompanied Coiffet to Tuzla to interpret, and spent three days there and in Kladanj. The refugees were in pitiful condition, completely drained physically and emotionally, and said that they did not have their menfolk with them. He was struck by the fact that there were only women and elderly men and young children, but no males of teenage or above. A few days later, he accompanied General Nicolai to Bratunac for the withdrawal of DutchBat from the enclave. Some time after that, he was awoken in the night and told that he would be part of a small group heading to Zepa to witness the evacuation of civilians from that enclave. He was to join two Joint Commission officers (JCOs) as well as Civil Affairs officers Ed Joseph and Viktor Bezruchenko to monitor the evacuation to ensure that it went differently from in Srebrenica. By this time, they were receiving consistent reports that a massacre or atrocity of some sort had occurred. The JCOs were to use sophisticated communications equipment to brief General Smith's military assistant, Colonel Jim Baxter, who would, in turn, brief General Smith. The group also included a French colonel named Jermaine and his interpreter, as well as a Ukrainian captain, a liaison officer based in Sarajevo. When the group arrived the same day at OP 2 at the top of the hill in Zepa, Generals Mladic and Tolimir, whom the witness had previously met in his role as liaison officer, were there. The witness's group and the ICRC representatives got permission to go down into the village from Mladic, who was in control of what was happening in Zepa. The witness asked Mladic if he could accompany Colonel Jermaine into the village, so he, Jermaine, Joseph, Bezruchenko, and the ICRC representatives went down. When they reached the center of Zepa, which was an open main square with a fountain in it and a mosque and houses around it -- I beg your pardon. They reached the center of Zepa, which was an open main square with a fountain in it and a mosque and houses around it. The mosque's minaret and some of the houses had signs of recent shelling on them, and there were shell craters on the ground. They made their way to the Ukrainian base, in front of which there were between 50 and 80 civilians gathered. A civilian doctor named Benjamin was occupied with curing the civilians and treating some injured men. The hodja associated with the Zepa mosque, a young man, clearly in no way a fighting man, was assisting in putting together lists of people. The Bosnian Commander Avdo Palic was also there and stated that they hoped they would be treated humanely, which the witness understood to mean unlike the menfolk from Srebrenica. He does not remember seeing any males from teenage up to age 50. As for the ICRC, though the witness has the highest regard for it as an organisation, this was one of the few occasions when he was frustrated with their attitude. It was obvious that the population was going to get moved out of Zepa and that there was very little they could do other than list everyone as they boarded the vehicles to make sure everyone who got on got off, but the ICRC representative flatly refused because she did not want to be involved in ethnic cleansing. It seemed to the witness that that was avoiding the issue and that things were going to happen, and since there was something they could do to make it better, then why not do it. The ICRC had virtually no further part to play in Zepa, itself, but said they were going to concentrate their efforts in Kladanj and Tuzla. General Tolimir gave permission to move out the injured men, some of whom had participated in the fighting, who were then transported in Ukrainian APCs and accompanied by Dr. Benjamin. The witness then returned to OP 2 in the afternoon and saw that haystacks, farm buildings and homes were being set on fire up the flanks of the valley. Later that afternoon, he returned to the village with the JCOs and saw that the number of people waiting to leave, consisting mostly of women and young children and some old men, had increased significantly. By evening, the first buses and trucks were sent down into the village, and approximately 20 vehicles of people from the square left in them. The vehicles had been arranged by the VRS. The witness spoke to some of the civilians, who were drained and wanted to leave Zepa without question. On a couple of occasions, when it looked as though the last truck of the day had come but then another vehicle arrived, there was a mad rush of people to get on, which was a clear indication that people wanted to leave. The witness was in Grozny in December 1999 and South Lebanon in 2006, and what struck him as different between Zepa and those places is that in the first two, while war always displaces people, the people try to leave at what they judge is the last safe moment to get out. In Grozny and South Lebanon, the last safe moment was before the place was actually captured. In Zepa, the last safe moment to the population appeared to be the moment that the fighting had actually stopped and the VRS were poised to enter the village. He is also fairly sure that the population had received information about what had happened to the military-aged men of Srebrenica. The war in Bosnia was a particularly brutal civil war, and what happened in Zepa has to be viewed within that wider context, taking into account it happened pretty much towards the end of it. On all sides, there was an immense brutality, and that was well known to the civilian population across the country. What sets the fear which the civilian population in Zepa felt slightly apart, but probably not unusual within the Bosnian context, is that it was fear of what happened once the fighting stopped rather than fear of the fighting itself. The next day, there were more people in the village, as quite a lot more had come in overnight. There was another incident of panic when some wounded were moved out in APCs and the population thought that that meant that the UN was pulling out, which caused the civilians to sit in the road and block the exit from Zepa. The witness tried to convince the people that the UN was going to remain there, and they also called up to Mladic to send down some more vehicles to show the population that the APCs were not the last evacuation. After the first day when the first group was taken out of the enclave, there were two full days in which approximately 4.000 people were evacuated. And then on the fourth day, there were approximately 400 people who left who were moved out. On this last day of the transportations, the witness saw General Tolimir in the village with a bottle of alcohol, slightly under the influence. Tolimir agreed that another group of injured men could leave, but the witness learned later that they were pulled off the vehicles in Rogatica. On that same day, the hodja was with the very last group of people leaving Zepa, but Tolimir identified him and said that because he was of military age, he could not leave with the women and children, and was taken off. The Civil Affairs officers protested to Tolimir, who said that the hodja could not leave. After it was clear the last civilians had been removed, the VRS soldiers entered the village, itself, and began looting and setting houses in the village on fire, which continued and moved outwards from the village for the rest of the time he was in Zepa. Rogatica Brigade officer Kusic appeared to be the senior officer on the ground at that point and participated in the looting, as vehicles laden with appliances, furniture and cattle were driven up the road out of Zepa. The Ukrainian captain -- I beg your pardon. During this time, the UNPROFOR soldiers were not permitted to leave the area of the base in the village. And the witness was in Zepa from 25 July through 2 August 1995. The Ukrainian captain who was part of the witness's group told him that shortly after the UNPROFOR representatives left OP 2, the mosque was blown up. When the witness raised this issue with Colonel Indjic, Indjic gave the flippant reply that it was destroyed because it looked like a missile from aerial photography. Mr. President, the Prosecution would tender Exhibits P742 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir -- Mr. Thayer, excuse me, I don't think that this was a short summary. It was a very long summary, and especially the part from page 68, line 16, until page 69, line 9. It appears not to be reflecting the evidence of this witness in relation to the events in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Oh, that's -- Mr. President, that most certainly is the witness's testimony. I just didn't preface it with such, but it is all the witness's testimony related to the events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Especially the formulation of page 69, line 2 to 9. There's no indication that this was the evidence and what the witness saw on the ground. I just want to mention that. We shouldn't discuss it any further, but we would appreciate to have short summaries so that we know what it is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Understood, Mr. President. I can assure the Court that everything in that summary is based, chapter and verse, and verbatim, frankly, from the witness's testimony. There is no input, no editorialising. Understood, it was too long for the Trial Chamber. But just so the Trial Chamber knows, it does not include anything from the OTP. It is purely his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That was not my concern, Mr. Thayer. It is only the question if that is -- if it is appropriate to have that as part of the summary read out in the court. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir -- well, first let me tender the associated exhibits, P742 to P754.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In relation to that, I have to correct my words at page 61, line 3. It is recorded that I said the number "6584" of the 65 ter list. It should be "6184." But, Mr. Thayer, you are now tendering some of the exhibits beyond that number. Are they really part of the 65 ter exhibit list?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, they are not on the 65 ter list. They were all part of the witness's 92 ter package, which has been provisionally admitted, and they are all associated exhibits. But given the Trial Chamber's instruction, I'll -- it will either -- I'll liaise with the Court Officers to see if it's a written motion or oral motion, and in what form. But, yes, there are a number of these associated exhibits that were part of the 92 ter package and which were admitted, but which were not added to the 65 ter list before we filed it. So those do fall into the category that the Trial Chamber noted earlier. So let me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you have heard the concern of the Chamber and the comments of Mr. Thayer. Do you oppose the addition of these documents to the 65 ter list?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we agree with your questions put to the Prosecution, and it is our opinion that we should really comply with whatever ruling you make on which documents can be admitted or not. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I noticed that you don't object to the addition of these documents which are not yet part of the 65 ter exhibit list. And if that is the case, leave is granted for the Prosecution. It's not necessary to file any motion in respect of that. It is granted, and now it is part of the 65 ter list. And all these documents with the given numbers are received as exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In addition to that, Mr. Thayer, three documents don't have a translation yet. These are P748, P749 and P753. They will be marked for identification, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: With those procedural matters, you should carry on with your questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions for you, sir. In 2007, when you testified last, you were based in Afghanistan with the Halo Trust. Can you tell the Trial Chamber, just briefly, what are you doing now?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB
utterances.text: I left Afghanistan at the beginning of June, and I'm now assisting Halo Trust with setting up a programme in Zimbabwe.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, again, just briefly, when you say "setting up a programme," what does that entail? What kind of a programme is it?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB
utterances.text: We're looking at starting a de-mining programme, so this is the very beginning of that process. So it involves liaising with senior officers in the Zimbabwe Army, the Zimbabwe government, trying to find donor money, so dealing with various embassies in town, and obviously getting out into the field to confirm the extent of the problem and its effect on the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to turn to your prior testimony for a couple of quick questions. You testified that you made the assessment that the VRS was a professional army. Can you briefly share with the Trial Chamber some examples of the basis for that assessment that you made?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB
utterances.text: I think part of it has to go back to looking at what were the antecedents of the VRS, and that was obviously the Yugoslav National Army, which was definitely a professional army with a professional officer corps. Probably, it was established largely for defence of Yugoslavia rather than as an attacking force, but it was based around various units in charge of a particular section of territory, with a degree of local command and the ability from headquarters to detach senior commanders to oversee particular incidents or battles. Likewise, there was conscription in the former Yugoslavia, which meant that most men of a certain age had a degree of military training, and through that military training, were used to command structures, discipline, weapon handling, and various other basic fundamentals of military life. On the break-up of Yugoslavia, and looking at Bosnia in particular, I think it's fair to say that the VRS benefitted most in terms of the highest number of professional officers and also the greatest quantity of equipment in the form of heavy weaponry, tanks, artillery, et cetera. Looking at the performance on the ground, it's important to note that we weren't talking about small groups of troops fighting, without much unified command. Within Bosnia, we actually saw the sort of deployment and employment of what we would call an all-arms battle; i.e., it wasn't just people with small arms, but a far greater degree of tactical ability was required. And, thus, we saw -- combined with infantry units, we saw tanks providing direct fire, artillery and mortars providing indirect fire, logistics, medical backup, all sorts of various other things which were well co-ordinated together, which gives us an indication that it was a professional force with a clear command and control, and that orders passed from the top were actually implemented lower down to ensure that all these various all-arms elements functioned together as an effective force, which clearly it did. I guess it's also worth looking at the spread of operations from across from Banja Luka, in the west, to Gorazde, in the east, and again it's an indication that the command structure of the VRS was able to, you know, manage itself effectively over such a wide area. So I think there's little doubt that it was a professional force.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you just referred to tanks providing direct fire. You testified in the Popovic trial about learning that a JCO, a Joint Commission officer, had come under direct VRS tank fire during the VRS attack on Srebrenica. Can you tell the Trial Chamber how you came across that particular piece of information?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB
utterances.text: Within the residency in Sarajevo, i.e., the BiH Command, the JCO operations room was literally just across a small sort of wooden plank-way from my office, and I happened to be in the area and was in a position to hear the conversation being conducted by radio between the JCO team on the ground and the JCO commander, and I think the air operations commander was also there in the room in Sarajevo, so I heard it directly on the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just tell the Trial Chamber, what exactly do you recall hearing during this conversation? What was going on that you overheard?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB
utterances.text: This particular JCO group had been extracted from the main command group of the Dutch Battalion in Srebrenica and was operating at some remove from the town, itself. They had come under direct tank fire onto their bunker. And at the time I caught the conversation, this was going on, and they were trying to call in air support for a -- or close air support to neutralise the tank that was firing on their position. They were informed that there would be some delay until the aircraft arrived. When the aircraft came, I think they missed on the first pass, but hit the tank on the second pass, which removed the immediate threat to that particular team. It was also quite interesting: There was frustration in the air operations command, because I think -- I could hear one side of the conversation, but I understood that simultaneous to this particular engagement, there was a threat to DutchBat, I think coming from General Mladic, saying, If you don't call off your aircraft, I'm going to attack your Dutch Battalion. And so we had one lot of people speaking to their officer commanding, saying, Please stop these aircraft, and you had another man on the ground saying, Bring them on, I need aircraft. And they were saying, Please, can someone step in here and tell me what's going on? I'm getting two conflicting messages. But once the tank had been neutralised, this particular group withdrew to B Company, Dutch B company, and then back to the main body.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall hearing any particular code-name being employed by the JCOs [indiscernible]?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB
utterances.text: I think the -- I think the call sign of that particular group was "Windmill 3."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Turning your attention to your time in Zepa, you testified about your experience with the ICRC representative who was on the ground in Zepa while you were there. Do you have any recollection of the UNHCR having any presence during that time?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB
utterances.text: No, I don't. I'm confident that when we went down, the ICRC were there, and the only two representatives of -- to the UN civil side was Ed Joseph and Viktor Bezruchenko, both of whom, I believe, were working for UN Civil Affairs, not for UNHCR. And I have no recollection of UNHCR being there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Thayer. Witness, now you know the other party, the accused, has the right to cross-examine you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I wish the witness a pleasant stay in The Hague, and I wish to greet him, and also wish him a safe trip back home or wherever he's going. And I will have a few questions for him. Before that, I would ask the Technical Service to pull up the statement of this witness, 1D278. Thank you. Could we see page 2 of this statement. We have it in both English and Serbian. My next question will deal with the first paragraph. You can read it or consult it, and then I will follow it up with a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mentioned how, in 1991 and 1992, you attended a course for officers, where you were taught Serbo-Croatian. How much time did you spend in that training, being trained in Serbo-Croatian, and how long did the officers course take?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB
utterances.text: The Serbo-Croat course, itself, if I recall, was three to four months of full-time instruction. And the officers course, I presume you're talking about the Sandhurst course, I did the last graduates' course, which was seven months.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Tell us, please, after the seven months, did you become a professional soldier of the British Army, and were you promoted to any officer rank? And if so, which?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB
utterances.text: On passing out of Sandhurst, I was at a rank of second lieutenant. And immediately following the Sandhurst course, I went on to additional special infantry training, which lasted for another four months, I guess, and then I did some service in battalion before volunteering for the language course subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you assigned the rank based on the course alone or was it because of your knowledge expertise? I believe I forgot to mention that in my question.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB
utterances.text: The second lieutenant rank follows automatically on completion of the course at Sandhurst. There's obviously a selection to get to Sandhurst in the first place, but once you pass out of that, everyone who passes out is at that rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question is this: Before your arrival in Bosnia and Herzegovina, as you refer to it in your statement, did you receive any other instruction about the history of the conflict in the area and the British policy vis-a-vis that region, that part of the world?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB
utterances.text: On the language course, there was a British Army officer who had spent some time in the former Yugoslavia, so he gave us some detail on the history. Obviously, at the time, we were reading newspapers avidly, as we knew that was the part of the world to which we were going. Right now, I don't remember receiving any specific instruction on what was British policy, specifically, to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Which one did you complete first, the officers course or the language course?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB
utterances.text: The officers course finished quite some time before that, and the language course came up as a volunteer option open to anybody who applied, essentially.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that, as it wasn't sufficiently explained in the statement. In the second paragraph, page 2 in the Serbian, the second paragraph, line 1, you say: "I arrived in April 1995 and was attached to the Command Staff for Bosnia-Herzegovina." Earlier, in the first paragraph, it is mentioned that you arrived in Bosnia in 1993 and 1994. Is this correct? Is it accurately reflected?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I served two separate tours in Bosnia. Following the first language course, I deployed to Gornji Vakuf and spent my entire tour based in and around Gornji Vakuf. I then went back to the United Kingdom, spent some time in Northern Ireland, did a further language course, and came out to Bosnia a second time. I believe I flew out on the 1st of April and probably got up to Sarajevo on the 2nd or 3rd.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In the course of examination-in-chief, you shared your impressions of the armies you encountered and their level of professionalism. Did you have any prior knowledge about military strategy and tactics? Did you receive that training during the seven months of the officers course?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB
utterances.text: Just to clarify the question, of British tactics or Yugoslav tactics?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The tactics of the armed forces in the area where you were sent to.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB
utterances.text: I'm assuming by that you mean of Bosnia, former Yugoslavia. How much of that was a formal lecture and how much of that was just done in general discussion, I don't recall. What I would say is that prior -- particularly what I don't recall is how much of that we got prior to the first deployment. Prior to my second deployment, I had also looked at going out as a UN military observer, and actually begun the UN military observers course, which covered that in more detail. It was while I was on that course that I got the offer to work out of General Smith's headquarters and, accordingly, accepted that second job. So, yes, I received some instruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement, you say that between November 1993 and May 1994, you were in Vakuf. What was your position there, what was your job?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB
utterances.text: My initial deployment was purely as a colloquial language speaker, and as part of that I was attached to one of the liaison officers who was working at that stage particularly from Gornji Vakuf, speaking to the BiH Command in Gornji Vakuf and in Bugojno. It then happened that the liaison officer, himself, had a recurrence of malaria and could not return to theatre, so I took over the role of liaison officer, spending most of my time then between Gornji Vakuf, Bugojno, once or twice to Donji Vakuf, and a couple of times towards Prozor, but I rarely got beyond that particular area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Given that you worked exclusively in the area where there were forces of the HVO and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did you have any insight into the tactics and professionalism of the Army of the RS?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB
utterances.text: At first hand, very little. I believe that there were VRS troops across at Gornji Vakuf, which I mentioned. I do remember picking our way across an anti-tank minefield to their position. But at first hand, beyond that, no, I didn't witness them in action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic. Mr. Gajic, I saw you on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think we have an error in interpretation. Mr. Tolimir said "the strategy and professionalism," whereas in the transcript we have reflected "the tactics and professionalism."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On page 2, in paragraph 2, in line 4, you say that you were a liaison officer and that you had contact with Mr. Zametica, whereas in the second line of the same paragraph, you say that you were also supposed to liaise with Lukavica. Which of your duties prevailed, was more important, the one that had to do with political representatives or the Sarajevo Corps?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB
utterances.text: To a large extent, that depended on where I was tasked to go by General Smith. We would have liked probably more contact with both sides, but the reality was that post -- probably late May 1995, it became virtually impossible to get all the way across to Pale. So from that date, which coincided with the air-strikes on the ammunition depots in Pale, it was pretty much impossible to get across and see Zametica face to face. Therefore, the reality was I would have spent more time talking to Colonel Indjic in Lukavica. But that was the way things panned out on the ground. Had things been different, definitely I would have been trying to speak to both parties as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I ask you this because in your statement, page 2, paragraph 2, line 4, you say -- regarding Mr. Zametica, you say that you were in regular contact, whereas Mr. Indjic was a liaison officer in the barracks: "He arranged meetings with Mladic and also took any complaints that we may have had." Can you tell us what had more priority, that you were in standing contact with Mr. Zametica or with Mr. Indjic?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB
utterances.text: If the message that I was meant to be sending was aimed at Dr. Karadzic, then the first attempt would be to do that along civilian lines, and hence Mr. Zametica. If the message dealt with military matters primarily, then we would try and go through -- if we couldn't get directly to General Mladic or yourself, we would be likely to go through Colonel Indjic. However, if one or other of those lines of communication failed, we would certainly try the other one, and hence I'm quite sure there would have been precedent for us trying to pass a message -- definitely there was precedence to try and pass the message to the civilian [Realtime transcript read in error "Muslim"] side by working through Colonel Indjic. And I don't remember a specific example, but it wouldn't have surprised me if we tried to pass a message to the military by working through Zametica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps there was a misunderstanding. Did you send any messages to the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: I'm afraid we didn't understand Mr. Tolimir's question. Could it please be repeated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the interpreters ask you to repeat your question. It was not heard properly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you send any messages to the Muslim side, through Indjic, ever, or was this mistranslated? Perhaps you thought the Serb side, whereas it seems to have -- whereas it seems to have been recorded as you saying it was the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS DIBB
utterances.text: No, it should have -- what I said related to passing messages to the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think we are at the end of today's hearing. We have to continue next week. It's the last hearing day of this week. Sir, that means you have to come back to the court next week on Monday, in the afternoon, I assume. Yes, Monday, in the afternoon, 2.15. You should be reminded not to contact either party about the content of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We adjourn and resume on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
